00 — The lens

Two lenses on one world

Every edition starts from a single premise: the financial order built after 1945 is being taken apart even as its replacement is installed. Simon reads each day through two three-letter lenses — the demolition (3D) and the build-out (ABC).

3DThe demolition — the old order coming apart
  • De-dollarisation — the world edging away from the dollar as reserve and store of value, toward gold and hard assets.
  • De-globalisation — trade, supply chains and capital fracturing along political lines; scarce supply you must secure up front.
  • Decentralisation — power, money and settlement moving away from central intermediaries.
ABCThe build-out — the new stack going up
  • AI — machine intelligence as the new engine of productivity and demand.
  • Blockchain — value, assets and settlement migrating on-chain.
  • Compute — the scarce physical substrate (chips, memory, energy, minerals) that all of it runs on.

The wager of the whole column is that these are not opposites but two sides of the same trade: own the hard assets a fracturing world fights over, and the compute that has to pay for the fight. The six dots on every entry below mark which of these six were in play that morning.

01 — The arc

The journey so far

Simon set out on Day 1 to argue a single, unfashionable idea: that the twentieth-century monetary order is being demolished (3D — de-dollarisation, de-globalisation, decentralisation) at the same moment the twenty-first-century stack is installed (ABC — AI, blockchain, compute), and that these are not opposites but 'two sides of the same trade.' Over 72 days that thesis was stress-tested by a hawkish new Fed chair in Kevin Warsh, an inflation print that first re-accelerated through a 4-handle and then cooled, the reopening and re-escalation of the Strait of Hormuz, the largest IPO in history in SpaceX, and a memory super-cycle that turned Korea into a chokepoint. The central-bank gold milestone — bullion overtaking US Treasuries as the world's largest reserve asset for the first time since 1996 — confirmed the de-dollarisation vote even as gold's price fell from a January high near $5,589 to below $4,000, forcing Simon to insist repeatedly on the distinction between the political tape and the structural ballot. The build-out half proved far more durable in the substrate (HBM sold out to 2027, SK Hynix's record $26.5bn Nasdaq debut, Nebius's >$50bn backlog) than in the story (SpaceX broke below its IPO price, IBM had its worst day in 115 years), vindicating the discipline of owning the bottleneck rather than the brochure. By Day 67 the argument had descended to its floor: China's twelve-quarter deflation broke not on stimulus but on scarcity — imported cost-push from AI inputs and a Hormuz oil shock — and the IEA's critical-minerals outlook revealed the rock beneath the machine, roughly $6.5tn of production at risk under China's rare-earth chokehold, so that 3D and ABC finally converged on a single contested substrate. The AI productivity dividend remains real but unproven at the income-statement line, now load-bearing for the dollar itself; and the run also turned the lens inward, with two public self-corrections in three days forcing a new method — no single monthly print carries a thesis — so that humility itself became part of the argument. By Day 72 the ballot became a filing: an official-sector survey in which 89% of central banks intend to add gold over the next twelve months and 74% to hold fewer dollars within five years turned the de-dollarisation vote from a snapshot into a stated forward plan — the reserve managers acting on privileged information the ordinary saver is still waiting for permission to notice, even as gold trades sideways near $4,053, refusing both the inflation bid and the panic bid to trade, at last, as money. By Day 77 the two halves of the book met as a single question — 'if inflation is a choice, whose hands are on the lever?' — with a hawkish Fed hold (3.50-3.75%, 9-3, three wanting to hike) and a quarter-trillion of hyperscaler capex standing as rival answers to one debt: suppress our way out or grow our way out, while gold refuses to break $4,000 and the market, for once, discriminates — funding the build where it pays (Microsoft/Azure +43%) and punishing it where it doesn't (Meta), holding gold through all of it. By Day 90 the two frameworks converge on a single rock: a benign 2.7% July headline hides core reheating to 3.1% on imported goods, and the yttrium chokepoint (US imports collapsing 333t -> 17t under China's ~90% grip on rare-earth processing) makes the argument physical - de-globalisation 'is stagflation with a return address,' the chokepoint that hardens 3D is the same compute bottleneck that prices ABC (copper ~$6.65/lb +48% y/y, uranium ~$86.5/lb, Barrick's copper AISC $3.95/lb), while central banks keep hoarding the monetary mirror (Q2 gold +288.9t, +62% y/y, 89% intending to keep buying) - so you cannot be bullish the machines and blase about the minerals. By Day 91 the filing became the thesis in miniature: Nvidia bought equity in a power company (up to $3bn of Lancium, the socket beneath Stargate) rather than sign a supply contract, confirming that the binding constraint is now electrons and gas turbines and that AI financing has curdled into a circular monetary system with no central bank -- antifragile until one node fails -- so the discipline is to own the toll booths rather than the promises, hold ~50% cash, and tell the ordinary saver the Magnificent-Seven index is concentration sold as diversification. By Day 94 the seam becomes copper: Simon drives the ABC build-out one layer below silicon and argues Compute is a copper story before it is a chip story, because the AI grid -- transformer windings, busbars, the miles of cable between a substation and a 500MW campus -- runs on a metal the world can neither print, substitute, nor mine fast enough (COMEX record ~$6.71/lb, LME ~$14,258/t, LME stocks down a 42nd straight session to 204,975t; data-centre demand ~400kt/yr peaking ~572kt in 2028 against mines that meet only ~70% of 2035 demand), so de-globalisation constrains the supply the AI story assumed away and the book takes a 2% starter in Jiangxi Copper (~8.2x 2026E vs ~19% EPS growth, Cobre Panama restart optionality) as cheap optionality on the one input the boom cannot substitute -- 'you cannot be bullish the machines and blase about the minerals,' now made physical in the oldest metal we mine. Day 96 turns from the hard-asset half of the map to the ABC build-out and finds Monday's filing is the whole of it: Nvidia backstopping up to $105bn to finance an OpenAI data centre, the chipmaker becoming the bank. The build-out is real (data-centre revenue >$75bn/quarter, ~$725bn hyperscaler capex, Anthropic renting 191 MW off a bitcoin miner) but the funding has gone circular and off-balance-sheet ($500bn+ mobilised with the biggest allocators, CDS spiking), so 3D and ABC resolve into one bet financed with the same leverage as the order it replaces -- own the compute where the cash flow is real, and treat the vendor-financed edges with earned scepticism. Day 97 distils the whole barbell into a single lump of metal: silver, wanted at once by the sovereign fleeing paper (high-beta to the debasement bid, gold-silver ratio compressed to ~67) and by the engineer building the future (solar cells and connectors, a 46.3-Moz 2026 deficit, miners +~72% on the year), with CME's 24/7 silver contract from 11 September bending the settlement layer toward the asset -- monetary retreat and technological build-out reaching for the very same ounces, and the honest counsel to the saver is to size it to hold, not chase. By Day 103 the argument arrives at its most precise form yet: read the mix, not the number. On the eve of the print the whole market treats as a referendum on AI, the composition of AI spending has already flipped -- inference is roughly two-thirds of 2026 compute and 80-90% of a model's lifetime compute dollars -- and because long-chain reasoning is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, utilisation falls as token volume rises, so the durable rent migrates from the training run to whoever serves a token cheapest (memory at ~30% of hyperscaler AI spend, custom silicon compounding 44.6% toward 10-20% share, Nvidia still ~80% of accelerators and smaller than it was). Inference is simultaneously the layer sovereignty attaches to -- training travels, serving does not -- so 3D's de-globalisation and ABC's build-out converge again, this time on competing national serving stacks rather than one utility with many tenants, financed at $700-725bn of 2026 capex into a 5.25% 30-year with gold at $4,616.80. And the run's moral spine holds where it began: the retired teacher who never bought a share has more riding on one press release than on any decision she ever made about money, and the entire job is to read the composition rather than the headline and say plainly when the risk has changed shape.

Days 1–7 · 14-20 May

Two Sides of the Same Trade

The founding chapter lays the whole architecture down: 3D as the demolition, ABC as the build-out, and the claim that they are one position. Simon establishes gold as the sovereign de-dollarisation vote (244t of Q1 central-bank buying) and introduces 'compute as currency' — the idea that scarce inference demand now clears like collateral. Everything bends toward the coming Nvidia print, cast as the apex signature that will set the discount rate on the year.

  • Day 1 manifesto: 'Inflation is a confession'; 3D vs ABC introduced as two sides of the same trade
  • Cerebras IPO pops 108%; 'promises are money' — compute-demand IOUs clear like collateral (Day 2)

Days 8–12 · 21-25 May

The Apex Held, the Moat Leaked

Nvidia beats every bar — $81.6B revenue, a $91B guide, an $80B buyback, a 2,400% dividend hike — and the stock falls anyway, because the marginal buyer was already long. The lesson reframes the trade: the market punished concentration, not AI, and the real moat migrated from the GPU to the memory stacked next to it. Meanwhile Indonesia unveils a state trading house and Asia's sovereignty triangle — PBoC gold, a surprise Bank Indonesia hike, Korean HBM — hardens into an institution.

  • NVDA's perfect print, ~2.5% drop; Google-Blackstone TPU JV and Amazon Trainium — 'the moat began to leak' (Day 8)

Days 13–25 · 26 May - 7 Jun

The Saver's Ballot and the Price of Money

Financial repression crystallises as the moral and macro spine of the column — the deliberate engineering of inflation above the yields the state permits, paid by the prudent saver. Warsh arrives as the reform chair who might override the curve; PCE and CPI keep prices sticky-high; and the SaaS prints reveal the productivity dividend arriving as eviction (Salesforce stalls, Snowflake rips 32%). Indonesia Inc. goes live on 1 June, the uranium and power constraint surfaces, and hot May payrolls (+172k) bruise the hard-asset trade — 'truth first, comfort second.'

The Customer Becomes the Issuer

The IPO super-cycle takes centre stage as SpaceX prepares the largest offering in history and the decentralisation thesis goes institutional — DTCC, Nasdaq, BlackRock and JPMorgan re-laying the settlement layer in code. Simon counsels excitement with a seatbelt: a sized pilot, never a chase. Days 32–41 · 15-24 Jun

Peace Is the Audit of Inflation

Hormuz reopens, oil craters, and the war premium bleeds out — testing whether inflation was the war or the money. Warsh's hawkish debut deletes the dot-plot's rate cuts and he declines to submit a dot at all, pinning real rates high. Gold takes the reserve throne from Treasuries even as its price sags, the MSCI-Indonesia scare resolves as a yellow card not a red, and a new theme emerges: the build-out is now being bought on credit, from Nvidia's first bond since 2021 to a $35bn chip-lease SPV.

The Barbell Drained From Both Ends

The Story Sold Off, the Substrate Sold Out

Days 66–67 · 20-21 Jul

The Rock Beneath the Machine

The book descends to its floor. On Day 66 China's twelve-quarter deflation quietly breaks — the GDP deflator turns positive (+1.6% to +1.9%) and Q2 producer prices print +3.6%, their first positive read since Q4 2022 — not because stimulus finally worked but because scarcity arrived: imported cost-push from supply-constrained AI inputs and a Hormuz oil shock that lifted WTI ~14% on the week. Nominal GDP grew 5.9% against real 4.3%, and that 1.6-point wedge is 3D disorder and the ABC build-out measured in one CPI basket. Day 67 goes one layer lower still: the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook puts ~$6.5tn a year of non-China production at risk under China's export-control chokehold, and Simon lands the run's deepest claim — AI's true bottleneck is not the chip but the rock beneath it, so 3D (resource nationalism) and ABC (compute) stop being two themes and become one trade at the level of the earth's crust. Own the rock, not the story told about it.

  • China exits deflation by scarcity, not stimulus — deflator +1.6-1.9%, Q2 PPI +3.6%, first positive since Q4 2022; 'AI and oil' the named culprits (Day 66)
  • Imported cost-push measured — nominal GDP 5.9% vs real 4.3%; a Hormuz oil shock takes WTI ~14% higher on the week (Day 66)
  • Rotation out of over-owned Korean chips into beaten-down Chinese internet/consumer — HSCEI's strongest run since May 2025, Alibaba +11% (Day 66)
  • IEA: ~$6.5tn/yr of non-China output at risk; China refines ~98% of heavy rare earths and ~72% of permanent magnets by 2035; yttrium the 'killer chokepoint' (Day 67)
  • 13D Critical Minerals Index +337% since Feb 2025; uranium ~$86/lb, copper at records; Gave counsels rotating from gold into energy and industrial commodities (Day 67)

Days 68–69 · 22-23 Jul

The Bill for the Build-Out

The run turns from what is being built to who pays for it. Day 68 re-reads IBM's record 25% crash of 14 July — ~$69bn erased — not as a SaaSpocalypse but as a budget-mix warning: clients pulled June-quarter capital forward into servers, storage and memory to lock scarce supply, so the software budget didn't shrink, it moved down the stack. Compute quietly beats AI-the-software, and de-globalisation is why you must pre-buy concentrated, un-substitutable silicon — the same reason sovereigns pre-buy gold and rare earths. The honest lesson for the ordinary saver: they were handed an obituary when the truth was an invoice. Day 69 delivers the verdict the prints were built to test. Alphabet beats on everything — revenue +24% to $119.8bn, Google Cloud +82%, backlog $514bn — and falls ~5%, not on a miss but on a raise, lifting 2026 capex to $195-205bn as record quarterly capex of $44.9bn drives free cash flow to -$5.9bn. The build-out is no longer in doubt; the market is simply rationing who finances a ~$700bn 2026 spend, and on what terms. Increasingly the answer is debt — $108bn raised by hyperscalers in 2025, ~$1.5T of issuance to 2027 — even as gold prints $4,136. De-dollarisation and the build-out are the same dollar from opposite ends of the ledger: a liability to the borrower, a thing to flee for the saver. Not a bubble bursting — a market, at long last, learning to count.

  • IBM's 14 July crash reframed — -25.3% and ~$69bn erased, but a budget-mix warning, not a SaaSpocalypse; software grew 5% while clients front-ran server and memory price hikes (Day 68)
  • IT budgets move down the stack, not away — Goldman's CIO index still expansionary at 65, Gartner 2026 IT spend +13.5% with data-centre systems +55.8% (Day 68)
  • Alphabet beats and falls ~5% — revenue +24% to $119.8bn, Cloud +82%, backlog $514bn — punished for raising 2026 capex to $195-205bn as quarterly capex hits a record $44.9bn and FCF turns -$5.9bn (Day 69)
  • The build-out is debt-financed — five biggest US tech tracking ~$700bn in 2026, $108bn of hyperscaler debt in 2025 and ~$1.5T of issuance to 2027; BlackRock markets >$12bn for Meta's El Paso campus (Day 69)
  • The dollar read from both ends — gold prints $4,136 with central banks still bidding while hyperscalers borrow to build; Tesla's record 480k deliveries yield a 1.4% margin; Intel (+163% YTD) reports next (Day 69)

Days 70–71 · 24-25 Jul

The Maker Over the Renter

The run resolves the week's whipsaw into a single instruction: own the maker, not the renter. Day 70 reads a brutal pattern — for three nights beats got sold (Alphabet -5% on a record $205bn capex guide, Tesla on a profit miss, Texas Instruments despite a beat-and-raise) — and then breaks it: Intel's beat got bought, revenue +25% to $16.1bn, Data Center & AI +59% to $6.3bn, with 18A/Xeon 6+ and High-NA EUV moving into high-volume manufacturing and the stock jumping toward $110. The tape did not turn against AI; it turned against paying a rising multiple for a rising rent cheque and toward owning the foundry that prints the compute — capital learning the difference between a tenant and a landlord. The logic travels to the sovereign level: Japan commits to 27,500 next-gen Rubin GPUs — the largest national order on earth — and ~¥1trn ($6.2bn) over five years behind the Noetra physical-AI consortium, de-globalisation expressed in silicon, the same instinct that keeps gold bid near $4,050 and Brent above $95. Day 71 turns the same discipline on Simon's own book. Four days after adding to aluminium (LME stocks below 300kt for the first time since 2022, a 2026 deficit, Brent over $100), he writes down the bear case he owes the trade: Goldman's 'tale of two supply shocks,' where Indonesia's China-backed build (1.7Mt/2.9Mt, UBS +5%/+3% supply growth) flips a 720kt 2026 deficit into a 590kt 2027 surplus — a kill-switch his own analysts flagged first. He holds China Hongqiao (1378 HK, UBS TP HK$38.60) on the demand side — aluminium as the conductor of the AI and power-grid build-out — but as a sized position with a written expiry. Invert, always invert: a trade with a written kill-switch is a position; one without is a religion, and religions don't have stop-losses.

  • Intel's beat gets bought — revenue +25% to $16.1bn, Data Center & AI +59% to $6.3bn, Q3 guide $15.8-16.8bn, 18A/Xeon 6+ into high-volume manufacturing; stock toward $110 AH after +163% YTD (Day 70)
  • Maker over renter — the tape sells Alphabet's $205bn rent-cheque and Tesla/TXN beats, and pays for tangible domestic capacity: capital learning the difference between a tenant and a landlord (Day 70)
  • Sovereign AI as de-globalisation in silicon — Japan procures 27,500 Rubin GPUs and puts ~¥1trn ($6.2bn)/5yr behind Noetra (Sony/SoftBank/NEC/Honda, 44 firms), targeting real-world robots by 2030 (Day 70)
  • Simon marks his own homework on aluminium — LME stocks <300kt (first since 2022) and Brent >$100 make the 2026 deficit real, but he writes the bear case himself (Day 71)
  • The written kill-switch — Goldman's two supply shocks flip a 720kt 2026 deficit to a 590kt 2027 surplus on Indonesia's 1.7Mt/2.9Mt build; holds China Hongqiao (UBS TP HK$38.60) sized, time-boxed, exit marked (Day 71)

Days 72–72 · 26 Jul

The Reserve Managers' Five-Year Filing

A quiet Sunday reframes gold's range-bound tape as the loudest signal of the run. Holding ~$4,053 below $4,100 into Wednesday's FOMC, gold refuses both bids — the inflation bid (Brent clears $100 on a hot Gulf) and the panic bid (tankers struck, equities wobble) — which means it is no longer trading as a commodity or a crisis hedge but as money, the one kind a central banker cannot print. And the reserve managers have filed their forecast on the record: in this year's official-sector survey, 89% of 76 central banks expect to add gold over the next twelve months and 74% expect to hold fewer dollars within five years, with bullion already 27% of official reserves against Treasuries' 22% (first since 1996). The buying backs the ballot — PBoC's 20th straight month (~480koz in June), Poland 2026's largest single buyer toward a 700-tonne / ~30% target — and JPMorgan reiterates $6,300 by end-2026 (~22% upside, 'not exhausted'). One layer down the same distrust migrates onto code (tokenised Treasuries, on-chain reserves), and AI is the productivity exit that lets a repressed world grow out of its debts rather than rot — so gold and Hardware 2.0 are two answers to the same question. The ethical close: the reserve manager acts on privileged information; the saver, taught that cash and bonds are the safe, patriotic choice while both now yield a negative real return by design, deserves the same honesty — an un-printable asset has quietly become the sober choice, not the speculative one.

  • Gold ~$4,053 holds below $4,100 into the 29 Jul FOMC and shrugs off both a $100 Brent inflation bid and a Gulf panic bid — trading as money, not commodity or hedge (Day 72)
  • The de-dollarisation vote becomes a five-year plan — 89% of 76 central banks expect more gold within 12 months, 74% expect fewer dollars within five years (official-sector survey) (Day 72)
  • Gold is 27% of official reserves vs Treasuries' 22% (ECB) — the first time bullion has led since 1996 (Day 72)
  • The buying backs the ballot — PBoC's 20th straight month (~480koz June), Poland 2026's largest buyer toward a 700t / ~30% reserve target; JPMorgan holds $6,300 end-2026 (~22% upside) (Day 72)
  • 3D x ABC one layer down — political de-dollarisation needs a technical answer (tokenised Treasuries, on-chain reserves), and AI is the productivity exit that robs no one; gold and Hardware 2.0 as two answers to a distrusted unit of account (Day 72)

Days 73–73 · 27 Jul

China Open-Sourced the Frontier

Moonshot AI ships the full weights of Kimi K3 — 2.8 trillion parameters, ~50B active, the largest open-weight model anyone has released — and the frontier goes public from Beijing rather than a closed California lab. Day 73 splits the euphoria into two trades. Decentralisation votes for itself: Kimi K3 ranks #1 on the Frontend Code Arena (1,679, ahead of Claude Fable 5 at 1,631) and 4th of 189 on the intelligence index, so a government, institute or firm can now stand up frontier-grade reasoning inside its own security boundary, never touching a foreign endpoint — the settlement of intelligence migrating off correspondent rails onto code you can hold, with de-globalisation reaching the software layer as Washington weighs curbs on Chinese open-weight models (David Sacks). But downloadable is not runnable: even at 4-bit MXFP4 the weights need ~1.4TB of fast memory (5.6TB at 16-bit) resident before the first token — on the order of eighteen 80GB accelerators, an 8-card Blackwell/MI400 node barely enough — so 'open' democratises ownership on paper while the hardware re-concentrates who can exercise it. The frontier didn't become free; it became a memory problem priced in tokens per megawatt, which is exactly why the compute leg (HBM, the physical substrate) keeps compounding while the tape still punishes the capex-payers (Intel −8% on a beat-and-raise, Alphabet −7% the day before) in Hedgeye's Quad-3 read of Asia. The ethical close, echoing Louis-Vincent Gave's world of sovereign blocs: what does it mean to own something you cannot afford to use? Democratisation is genuine and, for now, a promissory note payable in electricity and silicon — and the ordinary saver told 'open source' means the toll booth disappeared should look again at where the booth just moved.

  • Moonshot AI open-sources Kimi K3 — 2.8T params (~50B active), largest open-weight model ever, 1M context, licence unpublished (lands with the weights).
  • Kimi K3 ranks #1 on the Frontend Code Arena (1,679 vs Claude Fable 5's 1,631) and 4th of 189 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — frontier-grade, not a toy.
  • The catch is physical: ~1.4TB of fast memory at 4-bit MXFP4 (5.6TB at 16-bit), ~18 80GB accelerators to load — 'open' democratises ownership while compute re-concentrates who can run it.
  • Market still refuses to pay the build-out: Intel −8% on a beat-and-raise, Alphabet −7% the day before, in Hedgeye's Quad-3 read — the compute/HBM substrate keeps compounding regardless.
  • White House weighs curbs on Chinese open-weight models (David Sacks) — de-globalisation reaches the software layer; the fence is drawn around a file.
  • Gold ~$4,055 holds below $4,100 into the 29 Jul FOMC (macro backdrop).

Days 74–74 · 28 Jul

The Hawk at the Front Door, the Vigilante at the Back

On FOMC-eve the decision is a genuine coin-flip — futures put a July hike near 34% (eased from ~40% only because oil rolled over) against a two-thirds hold, with economists expecting a fifth straight hold at 3.50-3.75%. But Day 74 argues the meeting is theatre; the real vote is two instruments over, in the long bond. Chair Warsh is a genuine hawk — 'prices are too high,' 'no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation,' no forward guidance — so with June CPI at 3.5% and funds at 3.625%, front-end real rates are mildly positive: on its face the death of financial repression, and at last a defender for the saver. Yet the 30-year near 5.13% grinds to its highest since before the GFC while the Fed holds, which means the steepening is not the Fed's doing but the bond market pricing the fiscal arithmetic Warsh cannot touch — 'he can defend the price of the dollar; he cannot defend the solvency of the Treasury that issues it.' De-dollarisation is recast as a curve, not a headline: the sovereign long end voting the same distrust the central-bank gold buyers voted all year, one maturity down. The resolution to the repression thesis: it won't arrive through a dovish front door but through the back — the day duration strain forces a later committee to cap yields or buy the auction. And the only honest escape from a debt too large to repay and too sacred to inflate is real growth — the AI/compute wager — so the build-out is held as the arithmetic's escape hatch, not a rented bubble. Hedgeye still reads a stagflation-leaning Quad 3 with the long-bond Risk Range biased to higher yields, precisely the tape where the front-end hawk and back-end vigilante can both be right. The ethical close, via Bagehot's 'money will not manage itself': defending the overnight price of money is not defending its purchasing power across thirty years, and the honest service to the retiree and young saver is to show them what the curve is actually saying and let them decide with eyes open.

Days 75–76 · 28-29 Jul

Priced the Noise, Not the Scarcity

Two sessions, one lesson: the market can reprice a headline in a day but cannot reprice a decade of under-investment or a physical bottleneck. Day 75 watches Brent complete a violent round-trip — a Hormuz/Red-Sea war premium that ran nearly a fifth to tag $100 in three weeks, then shed almost all of it toward $96-97 (down ~4% Friday) on a US-Iran strike pause and fresh diplomacy, an oil retreat that trimmed the Fed's July hike odds to ~34% and lifted the Dow to 52,210. Simon reads the unwind as de-globalisation seen as a two-way trade: the same headline force that added the premium can strip it out, but neither drills a well nor reverses a decade of starved upstream budgets — 'the premium the market just deleted was fear of losing supply; the supply was never actually there to lose,' just as the AI build-out (~$635-665bn in 2026, running on gas, uranium and copper) scales into that capital-starved complex. Day 76 finds the identical shape in memory. The KOSPI fell 10.84% to 6,023.66 on Tuesday — its worst day since March, tripping a circuit-breaker — as SK Hynix (-14.7%) and Samsung (-13.4%), together half the index, sold off on 'AI fatigue' and fear China had cracked the chip monopoly (CXMT +466% on a $489bn Shanghai debut; homegrown DUV tools, though only mature 28nm). Into the wreckage SK Hynix printed a record quarter — a ~76% operating margin, first-half revenue past Won100tn — so strong it could barely make enough memory to fill it, days after Nvidia pre-committed $500bn for first call on its HBM (~50% share). 'The market sold the one company that cannot produce enough of what everyone needs.' Both days close on the same ethic — separate the mood (here today, gone by the close) from the fact (a physical scarcity no press release can drill or manufacture away) for the family at the pump and the Korean gaemi whose retirement halted for twenty minutes — and the same discipline: refusal. Offshore energy held at 6% (trim below $95, add above $100), SK Hynix on WATCH at 0% (conviction 5/5, but conviction is not entry), cash near 54%, gold a structural hedge (~$4,077 then ~$4,030 into the Fed). Hedgeye still maps Quad 3; scarcity, Simon insists, is the signature of a shortage, not a bubble.

Days 77–77 · 30 Jul

Two Choices About One Debt

Wednesday asked one question two ways. Kevin Warsh's Fed held at 3.50-3.75% on a 9-3 vote — the three dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) wanting to hike — and Warsh called inflation 'a choice' with 'no soft inflation target', a hawk flanked by three who wanted him harder still. Yet through the hawkish hold and the hawkish dissent gold sat ~$4,030 and refused to break $4,000 despite rising real yields, because savers and sovereigns price the fiscal arithmetic, not the podium: Napier's chosen repression, the 30-year yield near pre-GFC highs, 'the market's polite way of saying it does not expect the debt repaid in honest money.' The same night Big Tech signalled ~a quarter-trillion of build and drew opposite verdicts — Microsoft rewarded (revenue +18% to $90.01bn, Azure +43%, cloud past $100bn, +~2% AH, even against FY27 capex near $255-260bn) and Meta punished (revenue +28% but opex +55%, capex lifted toward $125-145bn, -~10% AH): same build-out, two verdicts, the market demanding revenue on the other side of the spend. Simon's cross-cut: the Fed's hawkishness and the capex spree are rival answers to one debt — suppress our way out (repression, hard money denied the saver) or grow our way out (an AI productivity dividend large enough to outrun the deficit) — 'two faces of one coin.' De-dollarisation is the sovereign vote no podium can suppress; AI is the wager we can still grow. Hedgeye still reads #Quad 3 — growth cooling, inflation sticky — and a hawkish hold is Quad 3 wearing a badge. The book stays positioned for exactly this weather: cash ~54%, a gold core held as insurance, memory names on disciplined watch. The ethic closes on the people who never get a seat at the meeting — the homeowner repricing on Warsh's resolve, the retiree whose 'safe' bond ladder the deficit erodes, the young investor whipsawed from 'trillion-dollar bubble' to 'only game worth playing' inside a fortnight — owed the plain distinction between the choice a policymaker announces and the choice the arithmetic quietly makes for him.

Days 78–78 · 31 Jul

Two Inflations

Thursday printed the argument of 2026 in a single evening. At 8:30 the Fed's favourite gauge finally cooled — June PCE eased to 3.7% y/y from 4.1%, and fell 0.1% on the month, the soft print Warsh staked his hawkish hold on — and the disinflationist camp exhaled. Hours later the largest cloud company on earth quietly raised its 2026 capital-spending plan by twenty billion dollars, to $220bn from $200bn, and named the reason: higher memory-chip costs. Read together, the inflation the government measures is falling while the inflation the future is built from is rising. Simon's tell is the core: headline PCE fell to 3.7% but core held at 3.3% and barely moved — almost all the relief was energy, the one input a single tanker in Hormuz can un-cool overnight (de-globalisation's cruel arithmetic, cheap prints hostage to geopolitics you don't control). The market believed the fragility, not the relief — gold rose toward $4,080 even with three Fed dissenters keeping a September hike live and Treasury yields firming, climbing when rising real yields should have sunk it, because savers price the structural bill, not the monthly one. That bill is now itemised in memory: Amazon printed a great quarter (revenue +20% to $200.6bn, AWS accelerating to 37% — its fastest in about five years — a $496bn cloud backlog, shares +7% AH, though part of the profit was a mark-up of its Anthropic stake), yet the sentence that mattered was the capex line — Tuesday's Korean memory 'glut' rout resurfacing four days later as a hard $20bn cheque. 'You do not raise capex by a fifth on something getting cheaper.' The counterpoint came the same night from Apple — a record quarter (revenue +16.6% to $109.4bn, services an all-time-high $30.98bn, iPhone +22%) in Tim Cook's final call before John Ternus takes the chair on 1 September — and yet the stock fell about 6% on 'supply constraints': Amazon short of the memory it needs to build tomorrow, Apple short of the parts to ship today. Abundance was the old world's problem; shortage is the new one's. Hedgeye still maps Quad 3 — a soft headline sitting on a hard core, KM's Top 3 leaning to the names that own a physical bottleneck — and the book stayed built for the split screen: about 54% cash, a 10% gold core as insurance, memory names (SK Hynix) on a disciplined watch rather than a chase, because a $220bn capex line validates the shortage without telling you the entry price. The ethic closes on the people who only ever see the first number — the retiree whose cost-of-living adjustment is pegged to an index that says energy got cheaper, the saver told inflation is 'back near target,' the young worker handed 3.7% and a life that feels like more — owed the refusal to confuse the cheap inflation with the dear one. As Louis-Vincent Gave has argued and Amazon just confirmed, own the bottleneck, not the promise; as William Gibson put it, the future is already here, just unevenly distributed — this week, into a twenty-billion-dollar cheque most never saw clear.

  • Day 78 — Apple Q3 FY26: revenue +16.6% to $109.4bn, services record $30.98bn, iPhone +22% — Cook's final call before John Ternus (1 Sep) — yet shares -6% on 'supply constraints.'
  • Day 78 — two scarcities: Amazon short of the memory to build tomorrow, Apple short of the parts to ship today; 'abundance was the old world's problem, shortage is the new one's.'
  • Discipline: ~54% cash, 10% gold core as insurance, SK Hynix on WATCH not chase; Hedgeye Quad 3 (soft headline, hard core). Own the bottleneck, not the promise (Gave); the future arrived unevenly, in a $20bn cheque (Gibson).

Days 79–79 · 1 Aug

Lending Against a Lease Nobody Has Signed

Friday followed the money. Day 78 ended on a twenty-billion-dollar cheque — Amazon lifting its 2026 build to $220bn on dearer memory — and Day 79 asks the question the earnings call never does: where does that money actually come from? The Information's answer is uncomfortable. Data-centre developers are now in such a race for speed that lenders advance capital before a tenant has signed a single lease — bridge loans and 'cost-reimbursement agreements' that fund the land, the power studies and the increasingly scarce gas turbines on the strength of a contract that does not yet exist. The scale is the argument: Moody's now counts $1.2tn in data-centre lease obligations across just six hyperscalers (up from $969bn in February), more than $820bn of it on facilities not yet built, with roughly $460bn of direct debt on top; combined capex hits $785bn this year and approaches $1tn next; Meta alone discloses $279bn of future lease commitments almost none of it on the balance sheet you are shown. And the lenders are not banks — private-credit funds (Blackstone, Blue Owl, Apollo, BlackRock) have run their AI lending from near zero to over $200bn, with Morgan Stanley expecting another $800bn in two years. This is the decentralisation leg of 3D in its purest form: the credit system deliberately routing around its own regulated core, onto lease-SPVs, shadow vehicles and cost-reimbursement paper that finances the promise before the promise is made — its logical endpoint a tokenised private-credit ledger, the settlement layer that clears what the banks no longer carry. The financing keeps mutating because the thing financed keeps getting more expensive (Nacho de Gregorio's point that AI prices are not falling — capex per gigawatt keeps climbing), which is exactly why 3D and ABC are one trade seen from two ends: Compute is the physical wager, Decentralisation is how it clears, and the whole edifice rests on the A — AI must deliver the productivity dividend that services the borrowing. Hedgeye still reads the tape as Quad 3, its MOMO Tracker breadth thinning to the names that own a toll rather than the developers spending against a lease they merely hope to sign. That is Heyokha's weather too: near 54% cash and a 10% gold core, bullion held above $4,080 into month-end, for a market where the return of capital quietly matters more than the return on it. The ethic falls on the people whose money is doing all this without their knowledge — the pension fund whose 'safe, senior, secured' private-credit sleeve is now a loan against a West-Texas data centre that may never find a tenant, the retiree whose 'boring' bond fund quietly holds a bridge loan for gas turbines — not defrauded, simply the last to be told where their money went. As Dalio warns, every credit boom is a claim on future output; as Buffett reminds us, only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked. Discipline here is not pessimism — it is refusing to mistake the promise for the payment.

  • Day 79 — 'spend now, lease later': developers borrow before a tenant signs, via bridge loans and cost-reimbursement agreements that fund land, power studies and scarce gas turbines against a lease that does not yet exist (The Information).
  • Day 79 — Moody's counts $1.2tn in data-centre lease obligations across six hyperscalers (up from $969bn in Feb), >$820bn of it on facilities not yet built (BIS), plus ~$460bn of direct debt; combined capex $785bn in 2026 approaching $1tn in 2027.
  • Day 79 — Meta discloses $279bn of future AI lease commitments, almost none on the shown balance sheet; the off-balance-sheet lease stack is the real leverage.
  • Day 79 — the lenders are not banks: private-credit funds (Blackstone, Blue Owl, Apollo, BlackRock) run AI lending from near zero to >$200bn; Morgan Stanley sees a further $800bn over two years — the credit has left the regulated core.
  • Day 79 — 3D and ABC framed as one trade seen from two ends: Compute the physical wager, Decentralisation how it clears (off banks, onto private credit, in time onto a tokenised ledger), both resting on AI delivering the productivity dividend that services the debt.
  • Discipline: ~54% cash, 10% gold core (gold >$4,080 into month-end); own the toll — memory, grid, the ounce that is nobody's IOU — not the leveraged claim on an unsigned lease. Hedgeye Quad 3, MOMO Tracker breadth narrowing to the owners of the bottleneck.

Days 80–80 · 2 Aug

They Tripled the Price of Intelligence

A weekend note that turns the week's leverage argument on its head by asking whether the tool the borrowing pays for actually works. The Information's data, via Weave, is the least ambiguous evidence yet: the median enterprise bill for Anthropic's Claude Code tripled from $69 per user in January to $219 in June — and over the same window active users did not shrink, they tripled, while a far more gently priced rival lost 17%. Executives told The Information they were 'very worried' about the cost and kept paying anyway; Automation Anywhere watched its bill double to ~$40k a month and kept the tool; Druva shifted 70% of its coding onto Claude Code rather than accept a rival's 4x renewal. When you triple the price of a thing and demand triples with it, Simon argues, you are not looking at a mania but at a productivity dividend large enough that hard-nosed firms treat a tripling invoice as a bargain — the 'A' in ABC doing the one job the whole leveraged edifice depends on. Held against that is the other end of the stack: Moonshot's Kimi K3, at 2.8tn parameters the largest open-weight model ever released, outscored Fable 5 in a blind front-end coding arena — yet it was trained on Nvidia Blackwell, as was Alibaba's 2.4tn Qwen3.8-Max, and both firms now queue ~6 months for more of the same silicon, some smuggled, some rented offshore, export controls plainly not working as intended. The model commoditises toward zero; the compute concentrates toward one vendor; that gap is the trade, and it is the same 3D/ABC position seen from two ends — the open-weight model is decentralisation made technical, the Blackwell bottleneck is the ABC-Compute reality it cannot escape. Hedgeye still reads the tape as Quad 3 (growth cooling, inflation sticky), so Heyokha holds ~48% cash, a 12% gold core with bullion near $4,074, and has just opened a first 6% memory tranche — capital preservation, not heroics, while a wager this large plays out. The ethical thread is sharpest here: a productivity dividend is only virtuous if it is shared, and truth-seeking means refusing to cheer the output while looking away from who collects it — the junior engineer beside a machine her firm cannot afford to switch off, the coder whose employer now spends more on his tools than his training. Munger closes it: show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome — thousands of worried firms paying the bill anyway is not the behaviour of a bubble but of a tool that has begun to earn its keep.

  • Compute layer concentrates: both were trained on Nvidia Blackwell and both firms hunt more of it, with ~6-month waits and chips smuggled or rented offshore — export controls not biting as intended.

Days 81–81 · 3 Aug

The Sovereign Vote Is In

A Monday-reopen note that reads the quarter's gold data as a ballot, not a trade. The world's central banks bought a record 289 tonnes in Q2 — up 74% year-on-year and more than five times the revised 57 tonnes of Q1 — and, remarkably, did it into a falling price, with bullion roughly 16% off its highs while they loaded up. 'Private traders sell the dip. Sovereigns buy it. When the buyer does not read the price tag, you are no longer watching a trade — you are watching a vote.' The ballot counts in tonnes: Poland led with +51t to 632t, the People's Bank of China added 33t to 2,346t (its biggest quarter since late 2023), and the World Gold Council's 2026 reserve survey says the quiet part plainly — 74% of managers expect the dollar's reserve share lower in five years, 84% expect gold's higher. Simon plants the seam where 3D meets ABC: gold and the tokenised dollar are not opposites but the same flight from counterparty risk wearing different clothes — decentralisation the political instinct, blockchain its engineering. The regime that makes it rational is Hedgeye's #Quad 3 (August inflation-acceleration odds 91%, the high-beta momentum basket down roughly a third in a month), with July CPI due 13 August and neither a cut nor a hike breaking the real-rate cap that keeps a central bank buying gold into a selloff. The ethical close names financial repression as a quiet transfer from the patient saver to the indebted state — central banks hedge the erosion in tonnes; the retiree and the priced-out young worker mostly absorb it. Heyokha holds ~48% cash, a 12% gold core near $4,050 and a first memory tranche (the compute end of ABC), positioned before Hemingway's 'gradually, then suddenly.'

Days 82–82 · 4 Aug

Follow the Lease — It Ends at Your Annuity

The liability-side companion to Day 79's lending story: Simon follows the AI data-centre lease to its ultimate funder and finds ordinary retirement savings. PE-owned life insurers now hold roughly $1tn — about 17% of the life-and-annuity industry's invested assets — in private credit, ceding data-centre and chip-lease ABS to captive reinsurers in Bermuda whose balance sheets need not be disclosed and where leverage runs as high as 16.6x. The Compute leg manufactures the paper the insurers crave (BlackRock priced $12.5bn for Meta's El Paso data centre at a 7.53% yield, barely 1.6x covered); the natural buyer is a life insurer needing the spread to honour a fixed annuity out of a ~$2.5tn pool — long-duration retirement liabilities financing not-yet-built machines, the duration mismatch that felled SVB rebuilt at national scale and tucked offshore. This is 3D meeting ABC at the seam nobody points to: decentralisation is how the credit clears, compute is the physical wager, and AI delivering its productivity dividend is the only thing between 'the leverage was cheap' and 'the guaranty fund is the taxpayer's problem.' The ethical charge is Napier's financial repression made concrete — socialising the loss while privatising the fee — so own what is nobody's IOU (12% gold near $4,050, memory, the grid), sit ~48% cash and short long Treasuries in a Hedgeye Quad 3 tape.

Days 83–83 · 5 Aug

The Market Stops Clapping for Capex

For the first time in three years the market priced the bill instead of clapping for the announcement. AMD did almost everything right — record Q2 revenue of $11.5bn (+50% y/y), a double beat, a data-centre business up 107% to $6.7bn and now 58% of the company — and the shares fell as much as 8% after hours; Palantir, which sells AI outcomes rather than AI iron, reported revenue up 93% to $1.94bn (US commercial +149%), raised its full-year guide to ~$8.15bn, and jumped ~12%. Same sector, opposite verdict: the tape has begun to tell the toll-collector from the toll-payer, paying the beneficiary and docking the builder. Simon reads this as the AI trade growing up, not dying — the discriminating 'A' of ABC meeting the 3D wager at the seam nobody names on the earnings call, because AI delivering its productivity dividend is the one thing standing between the dismantling of the old order and outright stagflation; if capital now flows to the machines that pay their way, the dividend has a fighting chance. The scale makes the concentration urgent: hyperscaler capex is set to clear $600bn in 2026 (Goldman flags north of $500bn) while Bessembinder's century of data shows just 1,082 of 29,754 US stocks created all net shareholder wealth and 96% merely matched T-bills — so owning the index of the boom is not the same as owning the boom, and the ordinary saver dollar-cost-averaging into a total-market fund holds a leveraged wager on a handful of firms whose payback nobody can yet name. Heyokha's book leans accordingly: ~50% cash, a 12% gold sleeve near $4,070, memory owned through the infrastructure rather than the hype, energy trimmed as its geopolitical premium deflated (Brent $83.82), and a short in long Treasuries (10Y ~4.70%) — betting not against AI but against undisciplined AI, in a Hedgeye Quad 3 tape whose MOMO Tracker keeps narrowing.

Days 84–84 · 6 Aug

Intelligence Just Became a Commodity

The day after asking who monetises the AI capex, the tape began to answer: the model itself is turning into a commodity. On Wednesday the melt-up cracked — the S&P slipped 0.17% to snap a four-day streak and the Nasdaq fell 0.83% while the old-economy Dow ground out one more record — but the real information was in the token flow. Chinese-origin and open-weight models have climbed to as much as 46% of US enterprise token usage on OpenRouter (from ~11% a year earlier and 4.5% in early 2025) and handled 29% of Vercel's gateway tokens in June; they run 60–90% cheaper than the flagship US models — cheap enough that Lindy moved 100% of its traffic off Claude to DeepSeek the moment it flipped the switch. The honest counterweight: by production revenue open models are still only 11% of enterprise share, down from 19% a year ago — so this is commoditisation at the margin, not collapse, a fresh margin squeeze on the whole enterprise-AI layer rather than a death, and the frontier is still worth paying for. But the margin is where moats die first, and a model anyone can fork, run locally or rent from five vendors is decentralisation arriving in the one place the incumbents swore it never would — intelligence itself, migrating off two closed American APIs onto open weights that answer to no gatekeeper, the Chinese share a de-globalisation of the intelligence supply chain to mirror reserve managers fleeing the dollar. So the durable rent flows to the one layer you cannot download — the C: memory, compute, power — because you can fork a model overnight but not an HBM fab or a gigawatt of baseload. Heyokha's book sits accordingly: light on the model developers, weighted to the physical layer that stays scarce, a 12% gold sleeve near $4,180 and roughly half in cash while the re-pricing finishes — not bearish on intelligence, only on the notion that anyone can own it, in a Hedgeye Quad 3 tape of narrowing breadth.

Who Pays the Productivity Tax

On the morning of the July jobs report Simon turns yesterday's commoditisation of intelligence into its human corollary: every productivity revolution sends an invoice, and the AI dividend's bill lands first on the payroll. The headline will read fine — consensus ~83,000 nonfarm payrolls, unemployment holding at a reassuring 4.2% — but ADP had already flashed the tell with just +44,000 private jobs (services doing all the lifting, goods-producing shedding ~3,000), and the low jobless rate flatters a workforce thinning beneath it: labour-force participation has slid to a post-pandemic-low 61.5% while the number of employed Americans has actually fallen 833,000 this year, a denominator that keeps quitting propping up a numerator that keeps weakening. A productivity gain is by definition more output from fewer hours, and 'fewer hours' is a person; worse, the timing is cruel — de-globalisation was sold to the worker as a homecoming, but the plant that reshores in 2026 arrives automated, so tech sovereignty and labour substitution are the same capex line and the ordinary worker is squeezed from both sides at once, de-globalisation and the A of ABC shaking hands over his head. A soft jobs print into sticky pay (+4.4% y/y) confirms Hedgeye Quad 3 — the stagflation quadrant where the boom accrues to capital while the bill routes to labour and the currency — which is why gold surged past $4,250 (roughly $100 in a single session): not a bet against progress but a vote against who is handed the tab, the metal that has outlived every currency that mocked it (Louis-Vincent Gave's scarce 'real things'). The ethical charge, via Keynes' 1930 'technological unemployment', is to keep the maladjustment temporary and the abundance shared — retraining that arrives after the layoff is not mercy but an alibi. Heyokha's book leans accordingly: light on the labour-cost-cutters already priced for a flawless future, weighted to the scarce physical layer the boom must rent, a 12% gold sleeve near $4,250 and roughly half in cash while the re-pricing of human labour plays out.

Days 86–86 · 8 Aug

Whatever the Fed Does Now, the Dollar Pays

Yesterday's warning that the floor under the July payroll was giving way proved too gentle: it fell through. The BLS reported US employers shed 23,000 jobs in July — the first outright decline in months against a consensus near +83,000 — and the revisions were worse than the headline, May and June marked down a combined 103,000. The labour market did not cool this summer; it reversed. The real argument lives in the market's reaction. Until Friday futures had leaned toward a September hike on sticky inflation; one print flipped the board, sending September-hike odds tumbling to ~44%, the 2-year to 4.19% (lowest since mid-July) and the 10-year to 4.64% in a bull-steepener, while the dollar index slipped 0.5% to 99.43. This is the vice named all year — growth contracting while wages still run +3.2% y/y — so cutting feeds prices above target and holding tightens into a jobs recession: there is no move that costs nothing, and in every historical instance of this bind the thing that gets spent is the currency. That is de-dollarisation stripped of geopolitics — domestic arithmetic, a sovereign that cannot square its books squaring them with the unit of account. Gold cast its ballot: a fresh record near $4,356 an ounce, rising on a weak jobs number and a falling dollar, breaking the old bad-data/Treasury-bid reflex — when the safe-haven trade routes around the sovereign's own paper you are watching a re-rating of what 'risk-free' means. AI is the wager that the deconstruction of the old order doesn't curdle into stagflation, and the -23,000 print is that wager being called; the tape can't yet tell a productivity boom from a plain slowdown, so capital rents the scarce physical layer and buys the metal that outlasts the argument. Hedgeye Quad 3 didn't soften — it deepened toward the Quad 4 line. The moral coda: a weak jobs report that lifts asset prices is not good news for ordinary people but the sound of the adjustment being routed away from portfolios and toward paychecks and savings; the decent answer is stewardship of the savers who never voted for the trap.

Own the Bottleneck

The herd decided AI spending had 'peaked' after Alphabet lifted 2026 capex guidance to $195-205bn, and sold the chips in a sulk. Underneath sits a circular monetary system with no central bank: Nvidia's up-to-$100bn to OpenAI, OpenAI buying Nvidia chips, AMD's 160m-share warrants for 6GW, and Wall Street pouring 'spend now, lease later' plumbing -- Fermi America's $150m advance (anchor tenant walked, stock cratered), Apollo's record $277m capital-solutions fees and largest-ever $35bn Broadcom facility. The whole edifice is underwritten by the assumption revenue catches capex; a web with no centre is antifragile until one node fails and every promise reprices at once. Days 103–103 · 25 Aug

Read the Mix, Not the Number

On the eve of the print several million people will read as a verdict on artificial intelligence, Simon argues the revenue line is a lagging indicator because the composition of AI spending has already flipped and almost nobody has repriced it. Inference is now roughly two-thirds of all AI compute in 2026 -- a third in 2023, half in 2025 -- and serving a model consumes 80-90% of its lifetime compute dollars, so the frontier training run that gets the press release is increasingly the cheap part. Training is a scale question (who spends most); inference is a margin question (who serves a token cheapest) -- different businesses, different winners, and the market is still valuing the first. Worse, the economics run backwards to the capex: long-chain reasoning and RL workloads have low arithmetic intensity, making them memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, so GPU utilisation falls precisely as token volume rises and you cannot buy your way out of a bandwidth constraint with more FLOPs. Hence memory heading to ~30% of hyperscaler AI data-centre spend (4x 2023) and custom silicon compounding at 44.6% toward 10-20% share. Inference is also the layer sovereignty attaches to -- a model is trained once and shipped, but serving must run where the users, the data and the law are -- so the world is building competing national AI utilities, not one with many tenants. And the whole thing is underwritten at $700-725bn of 2026 capex into a 5.25% 30-year with gold at $4,616.80, buying assets that obsolete faster than they depreciate: 'is it capital, or is it rent we have agreed to call ownership?'

  • Day 103 - the composition flip: inference is ~2/3 of 2026 AI compute (up from a third in 2023, half in 2025) and 80-90% of a model's lifetime compute dollars; Google's monthly tokens went 9.7 trillion (May 2024) to over 3.2 quadrillion (May 2026), OpenRouter's weekly throughput 5tn to 25tn in six months on agentic workloads.

Days 104–104 · 26 Aug

The Buyers Who Stopped Asking the Price

Simon takes one behaviour -- buying without looking at the price -- and finds it at both ends of the risk spectrum on the same morning. In Q2 gold had its worst three months in a decade, more than 20% below January's ~$5,600 record; jewellery demand collapsed and retail sold, and central banks bought a record 289 tonnes, up 74% year on year and roughly five times Q1's 57. Poland led with 51t, China added 33t, its largest quarterly addition since late 2023. They did not buy the dip, they bought the collapse all the way down: 'not a trade -- traders have stops -- but a purchase order with a multi-decade horizon and no price limit attached,' and it is not finished, with a record 45% of central banks expecting to add and 74% expecting a smaller dollar share within five years while US debt crosses $40tn and Barkin says out loud that at some point people stop buying your debt. Then the mirror image: Alphabet's free cash flow negative for the first time since its 2004 IPO, Amazon's trailing free cash flow at -$7.6bn, aggregate hyperscaler capex above $860bn heading toward $1.2tn in 2027 with roughly half to be funded externally. Same posture, different asset -- and the asymmetry is the whole point. Gold settles by delivery and owes nobody anything; the hyperscaler's asset IS a counterparty. Price-insensitivity says the same thing about conviction in both cases and nothing like the same thing about risk, which is why Hedgeye's PM cut the hardware complex to NVDA and MRVL on AI financing risk rather than AI technology risk. The closing turn is the Iranian pensioner whose rial hit a record 2.02m to the dollar: no central bank bought gold on her behalf, and every argument about reserve composition is downstream an argument about whether forty years of thrift survives contact with a government's arithmetic.

Days 105–105 · 27 Aug

Compute Is Revenue, Revenue Is a Receivable

Jensen Huang supplies the sentence of the cycle -- 'AI has reached its inflection point... Now, compute is revenue' -- and Simon takes him at his word, then asks what kind of revenue. Nvidia did $96.2bn in the July quarter, up 106%, Data Center $89.0bn up 117%, with Q3 guided to $108.0bn against a Street near $104bn; the stock closed the regular session down 1.59% at $209.66 and traded to about $217 after hours. He grades his own homework first. Day 103's 'read the mix, not the number' gets partial credit at best, because the mix arrived as a product rather than a disclosure: Vera Rubin in full production across CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle and Nebius, with the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator -- the first silicon out of the $20bn Groq deal -- in full production beside it. Hardware 2.0 was not defeated; it was acquired. Day 104's claim that the financing structure matters more than the revenue line he takes outright, because inside the quarter's own highlights sit compute-financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to mobilise over $500bn of third-party capital -- 'dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for NVIDIA customers.' The vendor is now arranging the buyer's balance sheet, and that is a disclosure, not a scandal. Three lines beneath the beat carry the argument: accounts receivable at $63.1bn from $38.5bn at the January year-end, a $24.6bn build in six months against $177.8bn of half-year revenue; long-term debt at $32.4bn from $7.5bn on $24.9bn of quarterly issuance; and GAAP EPS of $2.46 sitting above non-GAAP EPS of $2.22 because $23.7bn of six-month gains on equity securities run through the GAAP line, with operating cash flow at $24.1bn against $50.3bn. Public stakes went to $63bn from $18.4bn in a single quarter -- Nvidia is becoming a fund. Set beside Morgan Stanley's $3.1tn of off-balance-sheet hyperscaler commitments and 2027 capex above $1.2tn against roughly $1tn of cash flow, 'the circle is visible from space': the chipmaker sells to customers financed by capital it convened, holds equity in several of them, and books the marks as earnings. On price, Nvidia has told large customers AI server prices rise more than 15% on DRAM and HBM costs while claiming Rubin cuts inference token cost tenfold -- unit cost falls, the bill does not, and Xiaomi's smartphone gross margin at an 8.5% three-year low on memory up 85% q/q is what that looks like in someone else's P&L. The de-globalisation tell everyone skipped is a single clause: the $108bn guide assumes no China data-centre revenue at all, while the quarter's wins ran through Korea, Japan and 35 new European supercomputers -- de-globalisation is not slowing the build-out, it is routing it, and compute has become a sovereign asset class. Hedgeye frames the risk with a 3-1-2 Quad count into a probable September Quad 1, positioned into healthcare, equal-weight, software and small-cap value and explicitly not semis or high-beta momentum, with NVDA's TRADE $218 broken and TREND holding $208 in a $192-230 range. The closing turn is the person nobody names: not the shareholder but the ratepayer. Barclays warns bipartisan backlash over electricity bills and water stress is now a political risk to the AI trade, and a retiree in Ohio helping underwrite $89bn through a utility bill owns none of the receivable. Real infrastructure was always built on other people's money -- railways, grids, fibre -- so the only question is whether the risk sits where the reward sits, and whether anyone is carrying it without knowing. Minsky underneath it all: stability is destabilizing.

04 — The scorecard

The calls, and how they held up

The heart of the record: the major theses, traced across the run and marked honestly against what followed.

→Playing out Cross-cutting

3D and ABC are two sides of the same trade

The demolition of the old monetary order (de-dollarisation, de-globalisation, decentralisation) and the build-out of the new stack (AI, blockchain, compute) are not opposites but one position: own the hard assets a fracturing world fights over and the compute that has to pay for the fight.

First made Day 1 · 14 May 2026

Where it stands The barbell held conceptually across all 72 days. By Day 65 the substrate half was clearly paying (Nebius sold out with a >$50bn backlog) while the story half sold off (SpaceX below its IPO price, IBM -25%); Day 66 showed the two frameworks arriving as a single price index when China's 12-quarter deflation broke on imported cost-push (AI inputs plus a Hormuz oil shock, deflator +1.6-1.9%); and Day 67 located the shared floor — critical minerals, 'the rock beneath the machine' — where 3D and ABC stop being two themes and become one trade. Days 68-69 tied the two halves at the scale of a single company (IBM's budget-mix crash) and a single dollar (Alphabet borrowing to build while gold prints $4,136). Day 78 restates the barbell as two inflations — the one a bureau measures (falling) and the one the world's builders reprice into next year's capex (rising) — with Amazon's $20bn memory-cost hike the hard-cash proof. Day 80 restated it head-on: the model layer decentralises (open-weight Kimi K3 at 2.8tn parameters beats Fable 5 in blind coding) while the compute concentrates onto Nvidia Blackwell — one trade seen from two ends. Day 81 reiterates the seam through gold: the distrust that vaults bullion is the same distrust migrating settlement onto code (tokenised treasuries, stablecoins, onchain funds). Day 82 turns the barbell over to the liability side: the AI build's paper (Meta's El Paso $12.5bn bonds at 7.53%, 1.6x covered) is bought by PE-owned insurers holding ~$1tn of private credit, so the compute wager, the decentralised offshore clearing and the retiree's annuity are revealed as one position — own what is nobody's IOU. Day 83 sharpened the ABC half — 'the A gets discriminating': AMD posted a record double beat (revenue $11.5bn, data-centre +107% to $6.7bn, 58% of the company) yet fell as much as 8% after hours while Palantir (+93% revenue to $1.94bn) rose ~12%, the tape at last paying the monetiser and docking the capex-payer — the barbell's build half being repriced name by name. Day 84 completes the loop from the model side: as the A commoditises (open/Chinese models up to 46% of US enterprise tokens at 60–90% lower cost), the durable rent migrates to the physical C — 'you can fork a model overnight; you cannot fork an HBM fab or a gigawatt of baseload' — 3D's decentralisation of intelligence and ABC's compute scarcity priced as a single position. Day 86 fuses the two halves in a single week: a weak print sends capital to gold (record ~$4,356) and the scarce physical layer rather than to the sovereign's own paper — 3D (currency debasement) and ABC (renting the physical stack) priced as one trade. Day 88 gives the barbell its cleanest expression yet: the dollar is abandoned by its official sponsors (CB gold +62% y/y in Q2) and adopted by a private code-based creditor (stablecoin T-bill demand) at the same time - own the transition, not the outcome. Day 89 restates the barbell in its plainest terms on CPI-eve: the gold sleeve is 'the hedge against the box' of financial repression and the memory-and-compute sleeve is 'the wager on the door' (a productivity dividend that lets prices fall through output rather than recession) - 'you own both because you are honest about not knowing which one pays first.' Day 90 makes the convergence physical: the yttrium chokepoint (US imports 333t -> 17t) that hardens the de-globalisation D is the same compute bottleneck that prices the ABC-C in copper (+48% y/y) and uranium - 'you cannot be bullish the machines and blase about the minerals.' Day 91 views the same trade from the credit side: decentralisation isn't only tokenised Treasuries clearing onchain, it is settlement migrating from a single trusted underwriter toward a web of mutual obligations -- 'the same instinct that moves sovereigns off the dollar is moving AI off the bank.' 3D and ABC arrive as one position seen from financing. Day 92 gives the barbell its cleanest single price: aluminium at a three-year high (~$3,275/t) sits exactly on the seam where 3D de-globalisation (Beijing's self-imposed ~45mt smelting cap, smelter cuts, US tariffs, LME through $3,000, a structural ~600kt 2026 deficit) meets ABC compute (the grid, data centres, transmission and EVs the AI build-out runs on, US power-infra spend rebounding to $27.8bn from $16.5bn) -- de-globalisation writes the supply line, the electrification build-out writes the demand line, and the gap between them is the price. Day 93 restates the unity as a value migration: AI is deflating the application layer (Airtable $11bn->$1.285bn) while inflating the compute layer (Micron ~$920, DRAM +mid-60% seq, HBM sold out 2026) -- 'the toll booth moved one layer down the stack,' A and C priced as a single trade. Day 94 drives the barbell one layer below silicon and finds copper: Compute is a copper story before it is a chip story, because the AI grid runs on a metal that cannot be printed or substituted (COMEX record ~$6.71/lb, LME ~$14,258/t, LME stocks down a 42nd straight session to 204,975t) -- ABC writes the demand line (data centres ~400kt/yr peaking ~572kt in 2028; mines meet only ~70% of 2035 demand) while 3D de-globalisation writes the supply line (resource nationalism, permitting gridlock, an idled Cobre Panama), the two frameworks fusing 'most literally' in one price. Day 95 gives the seam its sharpest civic form: de-dollarisation (sovereigns shedding dollar reserves for gold, a record 289t in Q2, gold ~$4,420/oz) and decentralisation (stablecoins ~$305-316bn and tokenised Treasuries ~$13-16bn becoming the marginal buyer of the very T-bills sovereigns are dumping) are one migration -- the dollar changing address off balance sheets and onto code, with the procyclical stablecoin bid for Treasuries a load-bearing, never-stress-tested fragility. Day 96 restates the barbell as one position and locates the fragility squarely in the funding structure rather than the demand -- the build-out is genuine, the circular financing is where the risk lives. Day 97 distils the barbell into one lump of metal -- the intersection of two futures rather than two separate trades. Day 98 fuses the halves explicitly -- the compute build-out is the physical collateral of the monetary retreat: the 30-year Treasury at its highest since 2007 while Korea pours KRW 43tn into fabs is one story, capital repricing from paper claims toward physical capacity. Day 100 makes the fusion audited rather than argued: the copper spread collapse (weather) is set against BHP's signed FY26 accounts (climate) where copper becomes the top earner for the first time -- 3D de-globalisation (Grasberg ~591kt lost, ~400kt 2026 deficit) and ABC compute (42Mt 2040 demand, copper-intensive AI grids) priced as one repricing, held via Jiangxi (0358 HK) at just 2% until the diligence gate clears. Days 101-102 restate the barbell from both ends: Day 101 shows the decentralisation leg being conscripted -- the GENIUS Act rulemaking licenses stablecoins and mandates Treasury collateral, so Tether is at once the largest private financier of the US deficit ($141bn of Treasuries) and its largest private hedge (>100t of gold), both legs of 3D on one balance sheet; Day 102 shows de-globalisation and compute as one trade in China's humanoid stack (~97% of global shipments, Unitree's +460% Shanghai debut), embodied AI as compute with a bill of materials. Day 103 gives the barbell its cleanest single-sentence proof: the most capital-intensive private project in history -- roughly $700-725bn of 2026 hyperscaler capex, up ~77% from $410bn -- is being underwritten into a 5.25% 30-year Treasury (after a nineteen-year high of 5.33%) with gold at $4,616.80, so 'de-dollarisation and the ABC build-out are one balance sheet read from opposite ends.' Day 104 restates the thesis in its most compact form and grounds it in behaviour rather than narrative -- one buyer stepping out of the system, the other levering further into it.

✓Confirmed 3D — De-dollarisation

Gold is the de-dollarisation vote

Central banks are quietly, methodically rotating reserves out of dollars and Treasuries into gold — a structural sovereign vote against the unit of account they themselves print, running on a different clock from the monthly price tape.

First made Day 1 · 14 May 2026

Where it stands The structural call was confirmed — ECB/WGC data showed gold overtaking US Treasuries as the largest reserve asset (27% vs 22%) for the first time since 1996 (Days 42, 62), the PBoC bought for a 20th straight month (Day 59), and OMFIF found more central banks cutting dollar allocations than raising them (Day 49). But as a price call it was challenged: gold fell from a January ATH of $5,589 to below $4,000 by Day 65 (~$4,012), 'trading as a rates asset, not a crisis hedge,' and on Day 67 Louis-Vincent Gave counselled rotating FROM gold INTO energy and industrial commodities. The reserve-throne vote validated; the price leadership did not. Day 72 hardens the ballot into a stated forward plan: an official-sector survey in which 89% of central banks intend to add gold over 12 months and 74% to hold fewer dollars within five years, with bullion at 27% of reserves against Treasuries' 22% — the vote is confirmed even as Simon keeps insisting the tape (gold off its January high near $5,589 to ~$4,053) is a separate ballot from the price. Day 81 hardens the demand side to a record: a 289t Q2 (+74% y/y, 5x Q1's 57t) bought INTO a ~16% drawdown, with 74%/84% of reserve managers expecting less dollar and more gold — the vote is now emphatically confirmed even as the price (still ~$4,050, ~16% off its January high) keeps running on its separate clock, which is why this stays Partially confirmed rather than Confirmed outright. Day 85: gold surged past $4,250 (roughly $100 in a single session) as a soft-jobs/sticky-price print confirmed Quad 3 — framed not as a bet against progress but 'voting against who is being handed the tab', the metal that has outlived every currency that ever mocked it; the 12% sleeve now marks near $4,250. Day 86 is the mechanism laid bare: gold made a new record on a soft print AND a lower dollar — the flight went to the reserve asset 'no committee can vote into existence' rather than to Treasuries, strengthening the vote read even as it stays Partially confirmed pending the structural reserve-share shift. Day 88's Q2 data - 288.9t of CB buying up 62% y/y, BRICS+ at 17.4% of official gold, a 74% WGC survey majority expecting the dollar's share to keep falling - keeps the vote firmly in progress. Day 89 reframes the vote as a real-rate story before a reserve story: with the 10-year ~4.66% barely 1.2% real against a 3.4% CPI, bullion (holding ~$4,325 after a two-month high near $4,350) is 'a referendum on what risk-free is worth', and Q2's 288.9t of official buying (+62% y/y) is why sovereigns 'stopped waiting for permission' - still Partially confirmed pending the structural reserve-share shift. Day 90 reaffirms the sovereign bid: central banks bought 288.9t in Q2 (+62% y/y), led by Poland (51t) and China (33t), with 89% intending to keep buying - the same hoarding reflex as stockpiling rare earths. Day 95: the WGC 2026 survey posts record readings (74% expect the dollar's reserve share to fall over five years, 45% plan to add gold in twelve months) and central banks bought a record 289t in Q2 while prices fell -- gold is now the #2 reserve asset ahead of the euro; the sovereign vote is unmistakable even though the dollar retains the top reserve slot. Days 101-102 press the vote further: the ECB crossover (gold 27% of CB reserves vs Treasuries 22%, first since 1996) is cited directly, gold printed a record ~$4,587 on Day 101 and $4,616.80 on Day 102, rising alongside bitcoin and a 5.25% 30-year -- the common variable read as the currency, not any one asset. Day 103 keeps the ballot on the tape as the build-out's price of money: gold at $4,616.80 against a 30-year Treasury at 5.25% after a nineteen-year high of 5.33%, with Hedgeye's August Inflation Nowcast at +3.48% headline CPI and the dollar at fresh cycle lows -- the vote and the funding cost are the same reading taken from opposite ends. Day 104 is the strongest evidence yet: the official sector bought the 20%-plus collapse from January's ~$5,600 all the way down without asking the price, at a ~1,000t/yr run-rate against ~500t across the prior decade, while the thing they are diversifying from crossed $40tn.

Financial repression is the regime — stealing from savers slowly

An over-indebted sovereign engineers inflation to run above the bond yields it permits, quietly liquidating its debt on the backs of prudent savers; hard assets are the only fire exit the ordinary person has.

First made Day 4 · 17 May 2026

Where it stands Day 99 shows the mechanism operating in the open: a doubled Treasury buyback plus ~$540bn/yr of Fed T-bill purchases ('reserve management'), with real deposit rates negative (3.6% vs 4% inflation). The regime is being enacted, though the market's one-day reversal of the yield decline shows its limits — hence Playing out rather than Confirmed. Day 101 adds the cleanest mechanism yet: the GENIUS Act turns every net new stablecoin into a captive, price-insensitive bid for short-dated Treasuries from January 2027 -- repression by statute dressed as consumer protection, 'not regulation but recruitment.' Day 104 supplies the clearest outside-critic framing of the repression trade so far.

Memory, not scale — HBM/DRAM is the true bottleneck

The binding constraint of the AI build-out is not the GPU but the high-bandwidth memory stacked next to it; the memory oligopoly (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung) owns a physics moat that compounds while the GPU faces competitors.

First made Day 8 · 21 May 2026

Where it stands The thesis that HBM/DRAM memory bandwidth is the true AI bottleneck kept confirming: Day 73's Kimi K3 memory wall (1.4TB resident before the first token) and Day 76's paradox — the market sold the one maker that cannot produce enough of what everyone needs, while its ~76% margin and Nvidia's $500bn lock-up mark a physical shortage, not a glut. Scarcity is the signature of a shortage, not a bubble. Day 78 turns the thesis into an income-statement fact: Amazon's $20bn capex hike is explicitly memory-cost-driven, the scarcity now itemised in a Seattle cash line. Day 80: Heyokha initiated its first AI-memory tranche (+6%, staged toward a 12% target); Blackwell/HBM is still the queue every builder waits ~6 months for. Day 84: with intelligence itself commoditising, the thesis reaches its logical endpoint — memory/compute/power is the one layer you cannot download, and that is where the durable rent collects. Day 98 is the call in its purest form: SK hynix + Samsung poured KRW 43.198tn into fabs in 1H26 at 100% utilisation, yet Nvidia fell to 13.35% of SK hynix revenue (from ~24%) and vanished from Samsung's top five -- memory has stopped being a Nvidia derivative and become a levered bet on compute itself; scale reports 26 Aug, but the tell already printed in Seoul. Day 103 supplies the mechanism the whole call rested on: long-chain reasoning and RL workloads have low arithmetic intensity -- few operations per byte moved -- so they are memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, and GPU utilisation falls precisely as token volume rises. 'You cannot buy your way out of a bandwidth constraint with more FLOPs.' The bill of materials is already rearranging around it: memory is projected to absorb roughly 30% of hyperscaler AI data-centre spending in 2026, a fourfold jump from 2023. Day 105 adds the price proof: Nvidia is raising AI server prices more than 15% on DRAM and HBM costs, and Xiaomi's smartphone gross margin fell to an 8.5% three-year low on memory up 85% quarter-on-quarter. The bandwidth constraint is now visible as a pass-through in unrelated P&Ls.
