AI is the wager that 3D doesn't collapse into stagflation

The AI productivity dividend is the load-bearing assumption of the whole book — the only exit that grows real output faster than debt compounds, so repression resolves into renewal rather than robbery. AI when you can, else when you must.

First made Day 1 · 14 May 2026

Where it stands Unresolved by Day 67. The dividend is visibly arriving in capability but not yet clearly in the income statement — the 'AI budget problem' (Karp, Tesla/Uber caps, Days 54-65) and IBM's software miss (Day 65) show the invoice arriving first, and by Day 65 the market 'wants the receipt' at the 22 July hyperscaler earnings. Day 62 raised the stakes: record, largely unhedged foreign inflows make AI 'load-bearing for the currency,' and Day 67 set the deeper condition — the wager 'is only as real as the copper it can wire and the uranium it can split.' Day 79 raises the stakes: the unproven productivity dividend now services a $1.2tn-plus lease-and-debt stack, so the wager underwrites the entire build-out's solvency, not just its equity multiples. Day 80 is the first hard tell the wager may be winning: median Claude Code bills tripled from $69 to $219 per user (Jan->June) yet active users also tripled and a cheaper rival lost 17% — firms 'very worried' about the cost keep paying, the behaviour of a tool that earns its keep rather than a bubble. Day 83 named the seam explicitly — 'where ABC meets 3D': AI is the wager that 3D doesn't collapse into stagflation, and by starting to price the return on capex rather than applaud its scale the market gives the productivity dividend 'a fighting chance', with capital set to flow to the machines that pay their way; still a Quad 3 tape, so playing out, not yet proven. Day 85 lands the wager on the payroll: the productivity dividend is 'more output from fewer hours', and a soft July jobs setup (consensus ~83k, ADP +44k, participation 61.5% post-pandemic low, employment -833k YTD) into sticky pay (+4.4% y/y) confirms the Quad 3 quadrant the wager was meant to avoid — the dividend accruing to capital while the bill routes to labour and the currency. Still playing out, not falsified: the phase can stay 'temporary' (Keynes) only if AI's output gain outruns the displacement, which the tape has not yet resolved. Day 86 sharpens the test: the jobs reversal is the wager being called, and while the tape can't yet distinguish a productivity boom from a slowdown capital rationally rents scarcity and buys the metal — still Playing out, not falsified. Day 89 states the wager in one line - 'AI is the wager that this box has a door' - the only honest exit from a Quad-3 repression box (July payrolls -23k with -103k of prior revisions) being supply, not demand destruction: if compute delivers a real productivity dividend prices fall through output, and if not 'we live in the repression box for a decade.' Still playing out. Day 91 states the load-bearing assumption plainly: the entire circular edifice is underwritten by revenue eventually catching capex -- WhiteBox insists AI prices are NOT actually falling, which matters enormously because 'if that assumption is wrong, the loop doesn't loosen, it tightens.' Still playing out; the wager now underwrites a self-referential financing system, not just equity multiples. Day 96 sharpens the tail: the dividend still has to arrive to justify a build-out now funded on credit and vendor guarantees. Day 103 reframes the wager as a mix question rather than a demand question. Token volume is unambiguous -- Google went from 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024 to over 3.2 quadrillion in May 2026, OpenRouter's weekly throughput from 5 to 25 trillion in six months, driven by agentic sessions -- but because inference economics do not scale the way capex does, rising volume compresses utilisation instead of compounding it. The dividend is arriving as tokens served, and the market is still pricing the training run. Day 104 leaves the technology case untouched and moves the whole risk to the funding structure -- the first time a practitioner is shown acting on that distinction with money.

Day 90 generalises the thesis beyond Indonesia: China's rare-earth export controls (US yttrium 333t -> 17t, ~90% processing share) and the US counter (Pentagon 15% of MP Materials, $40bn-plus minerals funding) are resource nationalism as monetary policy on both sides of the chokepoint.

  • Day 105Day 105: the call is claimed outright on Nvidia's own disclosure. Inside the Q2 FY27 highlights sit compute-financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to mobilise over $500bn of third-party capital -- 'dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for NVIDIA customers.' The vendor is now arranging the buyer's balance sheet. Beneath the beat: accounts receivable $63.1bn from $38.5bn at the January year-end (a $24.6bn build on $177.8bn of half-year revenue), long-term debt $32.4bn from $7.5bn on $24.9bn of quarterly issuance, GAAP EPS $2.46 above non-GAAP $2.22 on $23.7bn of six-month equity gains, and operating cash flow $24.1bn against $50.3bn. Public equity stakes $63bn from $18.4bn in one quarter.

AI is becoming a budget problem — moat or money pit

The AI industry's acquisition tool was awe; its first churn risk is the invoice. Per-token prices fall while per-task consumption explodes, so corporate bills compound — every AI line item is now being sorted into moat or money pit.

First made Day 48 · 1 Jul 2026

Where it stands The audit visibly arrived: 'AI was a breakthrough, now a budget problem' (Day 48), Palantir's Karp saying enterprises are 'livid... paying for tokens that create no value' (Day 54), Tesla capping AI spend at $200/week and Uber at $1,500/month (Day 54), and IBM's -25% crash on slipped software deals (Day 65). Day 66 lifted the invoice to the macro level — the AI stack 'reprices its own inputs faster than it delivers its dividend,' and that imported cost-push helped snap China's 12-quarter deflation (PPI +3.6%, first positive since Q4 2022). Day 69's Alphabet reaction — punished for raising capex, not for missing — is the sharpest evidence yet that the market has begun pricing the build-out as a budget problem. Day 83 is the market beginning to act on the question, not just pose it: AMD's record beat was punished (~8% after hours) while Palantir's monetisation was rewarded (~12%), Chris Wood (Jefferies) was blunt that it is 'completely unclear who's going to monetize' the >$600bn of 2026 hyperscaler capex, and Bessembinder's century study (just 1,082 of 29,754 US stocks made all net shareholder wealth; 96% matched T-bills) underlined how brutally few will win — moat-or-money-pit is now being priced. Day 84 adds the commoditisation risk directly: token volume racing ahead of revenue and price-per-token flattening as open models undercut the flagships 60–90% — the margin, where moats die first, is now visibly under pressure, even as incumbents keep the frontier and the production revenue.

How it evolved (12 moments)
  • Day 48The Information — 'AI was a breakthrough, now a budget problem'; Anthropic raising prices.
  • Day 54Karp: enterprises 'livid'; Tesla/Uber cap AI spend — 'the bubble being invoiced.'
  • Day 65IBM -25% (worst day in 115 years) as clients redirect capex to hardware; software deals don't close.
  • Day 66The invoice goes macro — AI input scarcity becomes imported cost-push, lifting China's PPI to its first positive print since 2022.
  • Day 69Clearest confirmation yet — Alphabet beat on revenue, cloud and backlog and still fell ~5% purely on a capex raise to $195-205bn as free cash flow went to -$5.9bn; 'the market answered: not at these multiples, not with cash flow going backwards.'
  • Day 70Four beats, three sold, one bought in a week: the market stops paying a rising multiple for rising rent and starts paying for foundries/makers — Intel's DC&AI +59% to $6.3bn got bought while hyperscaler capex got sold.
  • Day 73Day 73: the tape still won't pay the capex-payers — Intel −8% on a beat-and-raise, Alphabet −7% the day before — even as open-weighting the frontier makes the build-out the only thing that matters.
  • Day 76Day 76: 'AI fatigue' names the money-pit worry — who funds the build-out — but the record memory margin and the pre-committed HBM demand argue moat over money-pit for the substrate layer, even as the software layer heads toward near-zero margin (the SaaSpocalypse funding the Hardware 2.0 boom).
  • Day 77Day 77 is the cleanest print of the thesis: same build-out, two verdicts. MSFT +~2% AH (revenue +18% to $90.01bn, Azure +43%, cloud past $100bn) vs Meta -~10% AH (revenue +28% but opex +55%). 'The market has stopped buying AI capex as a slogan; it now demands to see the revenue on the other side of the spend.' Discrimination, not euphoria.
  • Day 78Day 78: the discrimination continues — Amazon's capex hike is forgiven because AWS is accelerating (37%, backlog $496bn, +7% AH), the payer that can charge for compute; the market keeps rewarding spend that shows revenue on the other side.
  • Day 84Day 84: the margin side of the budget problem surfaces — open/Chinese models at 60–90% lower cost push open share to as much as 46% of US enterprise tokens (OpenRouter) and 29% of Vercel's June gateway, flattening price per token and squeezing the enterprise-AI layer's margin, even though open models are still only 11% of production revenue (down from 19% a year ago). Commoditisation at the margin is exactly where a moat becomes a money pit.
  • Day 87The margin question sharpens - open models ~35x cheaper ($0.14 vs $5.00 per M input tokens) now carry ~58% of US-routed OpenRouter tokens, hollowing the frontier-lab margin the index has already paid for.

The cell outvotes the barrel — China electrifies off oil

China is engineering its own way off the barrel — over half its December heavy-truck sales were electric — and controls the battery chokepoint; the pick-and-shovel is the cell supplier (CATL), not the carmaker.

The SaaS eviction — AI compresses the seat-licence layer

The AI productivity dividend arrives first as the eviction of seat-licence revenue (the layer above the model) and only later as growth at the bottleneck below; the consumption meter beats the seat-licence chair.

First made Day 13 · 26 May 2026

Where it stands Illustrated on Day 15: Salesforce beat but went nowhere on a soft guide while Snowflake (a consumption meter) ripped 32% on a $6bn AWS pact — the meter-vs-chair split played out in one evening. IBM's software miss on Day 65 (deals not closing as clients bought hardware) extended it, though this remains a thesis-in-progress rather than a fully resolved call. Day 68 adds a caveat: the IBM-led software crash was capex shifting down the stack, not a clean seat-licence eviction, so the eviction thesis holds only at the margin. Day 80: usage-based Claude Code billing triples heavy-user invoices as the seat-licence layer compresses — Druva shifted 70% of its coding onto it. Day 93 upgrades this to Confirmed: the seat-licence layer is being re-rated in the open -- Airtable's $11bn->$1.285bn markdown despite 20% ARR growth is the eviction in a single transaction, and the comp dispersion (25-30x AI-native vs 1-4x undifferentiated) is the K-shape priced.

How it evolved (5 moments)
  • Day 14Buyers shorten SaaS contracts (NRR down ~15pts) to free budget for Anthropic/OpenAI — 'the meter, not the chair.'
  • Day 15Salesforce beats and stalls; Snowflake rips 32% — the dividend lands in the rails, not the toll-booth.
  • Day 65IBM software deals slip as capex is redirected to hardware.
  • Day 68The SaaSpocalypse selloff (Workday -9%, ServiceNow -6%, IGV -4%) reframed — the software line didn't die, the silicon ate the budget; a budget-mix warning, not proof of eviction. 'Re-underwrite IBM; do not extrapolate a universal SaaS collapse.'
  • Day 93Day 93 is the call made concrete: Airtable -- an $11bn darling in Dec 2021 -- sold to Bending Spoons for a $1.285bn EV while ARR grew ~20% to ~$480m; the company got bigger and the price collapsed. Public software now shows the K-shape openly (AI-native 25-30x EV/rev vs undifferentiated seat-based 1-4x), 68% of CIOs are consolidating vendors and app counts fell 289->254 -- roughly five seats retire per capable agent.

Short long-duration Treasuries into repression

The deficit issues the supply, repression caps the yield, and the saver eats the gap — stay short long-duration government paper (TLT) as the operational expression of the repression regime.

First made Day 7 · 20 May 2026

Where it stands The repression thesis behind the short is intact, but Day 99's Treasury buyback announcement makes an outright long-duration short poor risk-reward near-term; the position was trimmed to -1.5%. Directionally right, tactically capped by intervention. Day 103: the 30-year at 5.25%, after a nineteen-year high of 5.33%, is the clearest confirmation of the repression trade's direction -- and the rate at which the largest private capex programme in history is being financed. Day 104 keeps the tactical cap in place (the buybacks are the intervention) while strengthening the structural case behind the short.

Intelligence is commoditising - the open-weight defection

The model layer is turning into a commodity and de-globalising along sovereign lines: open-weight, Chinese-origin models are roughly 35x cheaper and now carry the majority of the tokens US firms route on OpenRouter, so the copyable algorithm earns thinning rent while the durable rent migrates to the physical layer (memory, compute, power) that a hundred sovereigns each want to own.

First made Day 84 · 6 Aug 2026

Where it stands Day 87 ('The Great AI Defection'): Chinese-origin models set a record ~58% of US-routed OpenRouter tokens (briefly 63% in early July) as the US share collapsed from ~70% a year ago to ~30%; DeepSeek is the single largest vendor (~17.6%) ahead of any American lab, Qwen next (~13.9%), at ~35x lower cost ($0.14 vs $5.00 per M input tokens). Sovereign fracture confirmed by 100+ nations' Bangkok Declaration and national stacks on Qwen/DeepSeek; the embargo proves porous (Kimi K3 trained on smuggled Blackwell). Commoditisation is at the token layer; open models were still only ~11% of production revenue as of Day 84, so this is a margin squeeze playing out, not a collapse. Day 103 extends the defection from the model layer to the serving layer and gives it a sovereign logic: a model is trained once, anywhere, and shipped, but inference must run where the users are, where the data is and where the law says it sits -- so serving, not training, is the layer sovereignty attaches to. 'The world is not building one AI utility with many tenants. It is building competing national ones, each with its own silicon, memory, power and regulator.'

How it evolved (3 moments)
  • Day 84Introduced as commoditisation-at-the-margin: open/Chinese models to 46% of US enterprise tokens on OpenRouter, 60-90% cheaper, Lindy shifted 100% off Claude to DeepSeek - yet still only 11% of production revenue (down from 19% a year ago).
  • Day 87Hardened into geopolitics - 'The Great AI Defection': share ~58% (briefly 63%), US share ~70%->~30% y/y, DeepSeek largest vendor ~17.6% and Qwen ~13.9% ahead of any US lab, ~35x cheaper; sovereignty multiplies rather than shrinks demand for the scarce physical C.
  • Day 103Day 103: inference is the nationalised layer -- training travels, serving does not, so de-globalisation lands on the serving stack (silicon, memory, power, regulator) rather than on model weights.

Caught in the act — self-corrections

Where Simon publicly corrected his own numbers. Kept visible on purpose: the point is a track record, not a highlight reel.

Day 61 · 15 Jul 2026
Caught & corrected: Claimed on Day 60 that June core CPI was 'stuck near 2.9%' and that the soft headline was purely an oil story. → June core actually came in flat on the month at 2.6% year-on-year (not stuck), and headline was 3.5%, not the 3.8% he had cited — inflation was lower, not stuck.
Simon opens Day 61 with the correction: 'I was wrong, and the number that proved it was public at 8:30 the same morning I wrote it.' He starts with the correction 'because the alternative is to start with a lie.'
Day 62 · 16 Jul 2026
Caught & corrected: Built the Day 61 column on a producer-vs-consumer 'spread' anchored to May PPI of 6.5% (producers paying ~6%, consumers ~3.5%). → June PPI fell 0.3% m/m to a 5.5% annual rate (vs 6.2% consensus), core eased to 4.7%, and — critically — May's 6.5% was itself revised down to 6.0%, so the anchor figure 'no longer exists.' The spread narrowed from both ends.
Second correction in three days; it prompts a method change — 'the monthly print is not the signal... no single monthly first estimate carries a thesis' — a rule he then holds himself to even when the Day 63 print agreed with him.
